subject: Communication
title: The 90-Second Rule
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The 90-Second Rule.

hook.text: Neuroscientist Jill Bolte Taylor discovered that any emotion — anger, fear, rage — lasts only 90 seconds chemically.

buildup.text: After 90 seconds, the initial chemical surge (adrenaline, cortisol) dissipates.

discovery.text: If you're still angry after 90 seconds, you're choosing to replay the mental story that re-fires the emotional circuit.

twist.text: This means the pause is everything. Waiting 90 seconds before responding can transform your entire reaction.

climax.text: De-escalation techniques — deep breaths, counting, walking away briefly — all exploit this 90-second biological window.

punchline.text: Emotions are visitors. After 90 seconds, you're the one who invites them to stay.

quiz.question: How long does the chemical surge of an emotion last, according to Jill Bolte Taylor?

details.summary: Neuroanatomist Jill Bolte Taylor found that the chemical process of an emotion lasts approximately 90 seconds. After that, any continued emotional response is a choice driven by re-triggering thoughts. This insight gives a concrete window for regaining composure.
details.whyItMatters: Knowing that the raw emotion passes in 90 seconds empowers you to wait it out rather than react impulsively during conflict.
takeaways: The chemical lifespan of an emotion is about 90 seconds
Continued anger beyond 90 seconds is thought-driven
Pausing during this window prevents escalation

faq.question: What should you do during those 90 seconds?
faq.answer: Breathe deeply, notice your body sensations without judgment, and avoid engaging with the triggering thoughts. Some people count, others focus on physical sensations like their feet on the ground. The goal is to let the chemical wave pass without acting on it.

faq.question: Does the 90-second rule work for intense anger?
faq.answer: The initial chemical surge does pass in roughly 90 seconds, but intense anger involves multiple re-triggering cycles. Each time you replay the event mentally, you restart the 90-second clock. The technique works best when combined with deliberate thought interruption.
